item.title: Trump takes aim at Republicans but says Democrats did a 'good job'
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: 'Democrats did a good job,' Trump saysByKoh Ewe, Alys Davies and Gabriela PomeroyPublished4 November 2026, 08:56 GMTUpdated 2 hours ago
US President Donald Trump has taken aim at Republicans and conceded that the Democrats have done "a good job" in the US midterm elections, as they take control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in a momentous win.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump derided Greg Abbott, who lost the Texas governor race to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, saying Abbott wouldn't have lost if he "hadn't become a RINO in the last six months", using the acronym for "Republican in Name Only".
The president said that if he had been on the ballot, the Republicans "would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"
But he also said that he accepted the results of the election, telling The New York Times that he was "absolutely willing to accept" them.
While speaking to the paper, Trump added that he would "look forward to working with" the Democrats.
"We'll probably work something out," he said.
In a separate interview with Fox News, he said he was "a little surprised" at the outcome. "I thought they'd do better," he said, referring to the Republican candidates.
"The Democrats did a good job. they fought hard," he told the network.
But he added that the Democrats would send "insane" legislation to his desk that he would veto.
"After a couple of months of vetoes, they'll call and they'll say, 'how do we get this stuff done?' And we'll work together," he said, adding: "I have the power of veto."
On Truth Social, he posted a photo of a red cap - the kind usually emblazoned with his Make America Great Again slogan - emblazoned with the word "VETO", in an apparent reference to his ability to block legislation in Congress.

item.title: Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins in Michigan to become first Muslim senator
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: Abdul El-Sayed thanks supporters for backing 'unlikeliest of candidates'ByNada Tawfik, North America correspondent, Reporting fromMichigan and Madeline Halpert and Christal HayesPublished3 hours ago
Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won in the battleground state of Michigan to become the US's first Muslim senator, following a race fuelled by withering attacks and inter-party disputes.
El-Sayed bested Republican Mike Rogers, withstanding an onslaught of attacks that included baselessly tying him to terrorism and a high-profile spat with a fellow Democrat.
Rogers, backed by President Donald Trump, portrayed El-Sayed as a communist, criticising his stance on Israel and his Muslim faith.
After waiting long hours, watching the wave of Democratic gains across the country, El-Sayed's supporters celebrated wildly when he took the stage to mark his victory.
Image source, Getty Images
The former public health administrator campaigned on a left-wing platform that included universal health care and a wealth tax on billionaires.
The win comes days after El-Sayed's Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, endorsed Rogers, the Republican candidate, just days before the election.
El-Sayed's supporters gave deafening cheers when he took to the stage, as they chanted his name in jubilation. A sea of iPhones were held up to take in this moment of history - a Muslim man elected to the Senate.
Several people in the crowd embraced, filled with emotion. They repeated his slogan back to him like they were at a concert: "Money out of politics, money in your pocket and Medicare for all."
On the campaign trail, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, described Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide and called for an end to US aid to the country.

item.title: James Talarico becomes first Democrat to win Texas Senate seat since 1988
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesBy Gary O'Donoghue, Chief North America correspondent in Austin, Texas and Brandon Drenon Published4 November 2026, 05:35 GMTUpdated 7 hours ago
Democrat James Talarico has won the Senate race in Texas, facing off more than $200m in opposition spending and creating one of the biggest upsets for Republicans in the midterms.
Talarico's stunning victory over Republican Ken Paxton marks the first time a Democrat has won a US Senate seat in Texas since 1988 - and helped solidify Democrats taking control of the US Congress in a wave of wins across America.
Talarico, a former schoolteacher, was little-known until last year. He made the rising cost of living under Republican leadership a central theme of his run.
Paxton sought to portray Talarico's views as too progressive for the state, and campaigned alongside Trump on several occasions.

In a further, historic victory for Democrats in the state, Gina Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott - one of the nation's highest profile governors and a long-standing Trump supporter.
At a watch party in Austin, the state's capital, there were jubilant scenes among Talarico supporters as TVs projected him the winner on Tuesday night.
Supporters hugged, they kissed, and they drank to a reality that many say they dared not believe would come true.
Emerging on stage to rapturous applause at his official watch party at a nearby performing arts theatre, Talarico pronounced: "We just took back Texas."
"We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas," he continued, referring to his win over Paxton whose campaign was backed by Elon Musk, the world's richest man.

item.title: Florida Republicans fend off Democrats as state elects first black governor
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesBy Jude Sheerin and Brandon DrenonPublished4 November 2026, 05:02 GMTUpdated 5 hours ago
Republican candidates in Florida have held off several high-profile challenges from Democrats, as results also saw the state elect its first black governor.
Republican Byron Donalds, backed by President Donald Trump, won the race for governor, while Republican Ashley Moody held her seat in the Senate.
She was up against Democrat Angie Nixon in the special election for Secretary of State Marco Rubio's old Senate seat.
The two wins came amid countless - and historic - gains by Democrats that gave them full control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate for the last years of Trump's presidency.

Nixon had scored a surprise win in the Democratic primary to become her party's standard-bearer, although her campaign funding could not match Moody's, who came out on top.
Donalds had served in Congress since 2021 before running for governor to replace long-serving Republican Governor Ron DeSantis, who was term limited and could not run again.
A big supporter of Trump, Donalds was at one point on the short list to be his running mate in 2024.
Born in Brooklyn, he moved to Florida for university and became a fixture in local politics before running for Congress.
Democrats in the state had some surprise wins, too. Republicans in Florida had helped redraw political voting maps as part of a national redistricting push to boost each political party's chances of taking seats in the House.

item.title: Iran's chief negotiator says Americans voted 'no to war'
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf said Iran "endorsed" the message sent by American votersByHelen Davidson and David GrittenPublished4 November 2026, 07:17 GMTUpdated 45 minutes ago
Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the US has said that Americans have "said NO TO WAR", after President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered a stunning defeat in the midterm elections.
"We endorse this message," parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X.
"If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," he warned.
Trump acknowledged on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in petrol prices. But he insisted that he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran in February.
Iran's Supreme Leader said he did not expect US policy to change after the results.
Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since the Iran war began, released a statement saying anyone who thinks there will be any change from American "hostility towards the Iranian nation" is "gravely mistaken".
In an interview with Fox News, Trump said of the midterm results: "I think a part of it was Iran".
He went on to say: "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that."
Speaking separately to the BBC's US news partner, CBS News, Trump said the conflict would end "when I say it ends".
In recent weeks, the president has warned that the US and Israel could return to all-out war after the midterms if a deal to end the conflict cannot be reached with Iran.
Also on Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: Delhi air quality worsens ahead of Diwali as firework restrictions enter force
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Air pollution is an annual problem in Delhi and large parts of northern IndiaByAbhishek Dey & Rachita PrasadBBC NewsPublished4 November 2026, 06:50 GMTUpdated 5 hours ago
Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.
The city's air quality index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.
Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.
Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.
GRAP is a set of emergency measures that become progressively stricter as pollution levels rise. The latest restrictions include more intensive road cleaning, higher parking charges to discourage private vehicle use and increased public transport services. Delhi Metro has introduced 20 additional weekday train trips, while authorities have been directed to stagger government office timings to ease traffic congestion.
Officials said the measures were introduced after forecasts suggested air quality would remain very poor over the coming days.
Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.
The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.

item.title: ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
More than 500 parties are contesting the electionsByKhanyisile NgcoboReporting fromJohannesburgPublished4 November 2026, 00:03 GMTUpdated 1 hour ago
South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's biggest party, the African National Congress (ANC).
This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes.
Election officials say voting is going smoothly, despite long queues at some polling stations.
Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.
For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.
Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.
At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.
Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral.
"What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.
In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.

item.title: Sharp objects found in Halloween sweets in three European nations
item.description:
Image source, Hannover PoliceByPaul KirbyEurope digital editorPublished35 minutes ago
Needles and other sharp metal objects have been found in sweets handed out over Halloween in Germany, Austria and Hungary, prompting police to issue warnings to parents to check what their children have been given.
Police in a number of German states have reported cases, from Bavaria in the south-east to Lower Saxony in the north.
A girl aged nine hurt her tongue while eating a chocolate bar in Bremervörde, west of Hamburg. A 5cm-long (2in) pin was then found inside it.
Meanwhile, police in Hungary have launched a criminal investigation after nails, screws and pieces of wire were found in sweets handed out to children who had been trick-or-treating in and around the town of Gyömrő, to the east of Budapest.
The local authority said one young girl had been handed a toffee with a nail inside a chocolate wrapper and that she had fortunately noticed in time and had not swallowed the sweet.
Several cases have also been reported across Austria, where Interior Minister Gerhard Karner condemned the incidents as "cowardly, malicious and in some cases life-threatening".
Image source, Gyömrő town council/FacebookImage caption,
A chocolate wrapper was used to hand a girl a toffee with a sharp tack inside it in Hungary
Police there said investigations were under way in four states, and that a 10-year-old girl had suffered a minor injury to her mouth when she bit into a small chocolate bar in the Amstetten area to the east of Linz.
Lower Austria Governor Johanna Mikl-Leitner said the perpetrators had to feel the full force of the law, adding: "Our children deserve a carefree childhood and we'll continue to ensure that."

item.title: Rwanda's army team removed from Africa league after US sanctions, NBA says
item.description:
Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Rwanda's army team APR came third in the Basketball Africa League last yearByBasillioh RukangaPublished4 November 2026, 10:19 GMTUpdated 1 hour ago
The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.
The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).
However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.
The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March.
The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".
Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.
The BBC has asked Rwanda for comment.

item.description:

Officials say this video shows escaped inmate stealing a truckByHelen DavidsonPublished4 November 2026, 02:11 GMT
US authorities have recaptured a convicted murderer who escaped a Tennessee prison more than a week ago.
Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was serving a life sentence over the killing of his colleague in 2022, when he escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, about 90 miles (145 km) north of Memphis.
The Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC) said security footage showed Morley, wearing his prison uniform, breaching the prison fence around 11:30pm on 25 October, and later stealing a vehicle from a nearby farm.
On Wednesday the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) announced Morley was in custody after an operation that involved local, state and federal agencies.
In a statement, the TBI said authorities had received a tip that Morley was hiding on an Illinois property, from which a truck had also been stolen.
The truck's licence plate was then tracked through automatic plate-reader technology, travelling through Missouri, where local authorities were dispatched to follow.
Morley was apprehended by Missouri State Highway Patrol "without incident" in Carroll County at 11:34am local time on Tuesday. Three firearms that had previously been reported stolen were also recovered from the vehicle, the TBI said.
Photos published by authorities showed Morley handcuffed and being led out of a field by officers.
Image source, Missouri State Highway PatrolImage caption,
Morley was apprehended by officers in Missouri
Following his escape, Morley had been added to the TBI's most wanted list, with the TDOC offering a reward of up to $2,500 (£1,900) for information leading to his arrest. The reward was increased by $15,000 on Wednesday.
